p.src: Now the two villains Li Jue and Guo Si wished to murder Emperor Xian. Zhang Ji and Fan Chou remonstrated, “You must not. If you kill him today, the people may refuse to submit. It would be better to continue honoring him as sovereign and lure the feudal lords within the passes. First remove his supporters, and then kill him; thus the empire may be ours.” Li Jue and Guo Si accepted their counsel and lowered their weapons. From the tower the Emperor proclaimed, “Wang Yun has already been executed. Why have your troops not withdrawn?” Li Jue and Guo Si replied, “We your servants have rendered service to the imperial house but have yet to receive titles, and therefore dare not withdraw our troops.” The Emperor said, “What titles do you desire?” Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou each wrote down the office and rank he desired and presented the demands to the Emperor. The Emperor had no choice but to comply. He appointed Li Jue General of Chariots and Cavalry and Marquis of Chiyang, placed him over the Metropolitan Commandancy, and granted him the emblems of imperial authority; Guo Si was appointed General of the Rear and likewise granted the emblems of imperial authority; together they controlled the government. Fan Chou was appointed General of the Right and Marquis of Wannian; and Zhang Ji was appointed General of Agile Cavalry and Marquis of Pingyang and ordered to garrison Hongnong with his troops. The others, including Li Meng and Wang Fang, were each made colonels. Only then did they offer thanks for the imperial favor and lead their troops out of the city. They further ordered a search for Dong Zhuo’s remains. Having recovered a few scraps of skin and bone, they carved a body from fragrant wood, fitted the remnants into it, and held a magnificent funeral rite. They furnished it with the robes, cap, coffin, and outer casket of a king, chose an auspicious day, and prepared to rebury it at Mei Citadel. When the day of burial arrived, a tremendous thunderstorm descended. Water rose several feet over the level ground, and a thunderbolt split open the coffin and cast the remains outside it. Li Jue waited for clear weather and buried him again, but that night the same thing happened once more. They attempted the burial three times, but on every occasion it failed. Every last scrap of skin and fragment of bone was consumed by the lightning’s fire. Heaven’s wrath against Dong Zhuo may truly be called extreme!

p.src: Now that Li Jue and Guo Si held supreme power, they brutalized the common people and secretly stationed trusted agents at the Emperor’s side to watch his every movement. At this time, Emperor Xian’s every action was beset with thorns. Every promotion and demotion among the court officials was decided by the two villains. To win public esteem, they specially summoned Zhu Jun to court, appointed him Grand Coachman, and had him share in the direction of government.

p.src: One day came a report that Ma Teng, Governor of Xiliang, and Han Sui, Inspector of Bingzhou, were advancing upon Chang’an with more than a hundred thousand troops, proclaiming that they had come to punish the traitors. It transpired that the two commanders had previously sent agents into Chang’an and enlisted Palace Attendant Ma Yu, Remonstrant Counselor Chong Shao, and General of the Left Household Liu Fan as their allies within the city, all conspiring together against the traitorous faction. The three secretly memorialized Emperor Xian, who appointed Ma Teng General Who Conquers the West and Han Sui General Who Guards the West. Each received a secret edict commanding them to combine their strength and punish the traitors. When Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou heard that the two armies were approaching, they met to discuss a strategy for resisting them. The strategist Jia Xu said, “Since the two armies have come from afar, we should merely deepen our moats, raise our ramparts, and hold firm against them. In no more than a hundred days their provisions will be exhausted, and they will surely withdraw of their own accord. Then we can pursue them, and both commanders will be captured.” Li Meng and Wang Fang stepped forward and said, “That is no good plan. Lend us ten thousand picked troops, and we shall promptly cut off the heads of Ma Teng and Han Sui and lay them before you.” Jia Xu said, “If you engage them now, you will certainly suffer defeat.” Li Meng and Wang Fang cried together, “If we two are defeated, we willingly submit to beheading; but if we win, you, sir, must also surrender your head to us.” Jia Xu said to Li Jue and Guo Si, “Two hundred li west of Chang’an lies Mount Zhouzhi, whose approaches are steep and dangerous. Generals Zhang and Fan should be sent to station troops there and hold its fortified positions; meanwhile, let Li Meng and Wang Fang lead their own troops out to meet the enemy.” Li Jue and Guo Si followed his counsel and assigned fifteen thousand troops and horsemen to Li Meng and Wang Fang. The two departed delighted and pitched camp two hundred and eighty li from Chang’an.

p.src: When the Xiliang troops arrived, the two commanders led their army forward to meet them. The Xiliang forces barred the road and deployed in battle formation. Ma Teng and Han Sui rode out side by side. Pointing at Li Meng and Wang Fang, they cursed, “Traitors to the realm! Who will capture them?” Before the words had left their mouths, a young general appeared, his face fair as ceremonial jade, his eyes like shooting stars, with the body of a tiger, the arms of an ape, the belly of a leopard, and the waist of a wolf. Gripping a long spear and mounted upon a fine steed, he flew out from the ranks. This general was Ma Teng’s son Ma Chao, styled Mengqi. Though only seventeen years old, he was matchless in valor. Wang Fang, despising him for his youth, spurred his horse forward to fight. Within only a few exchanges, Ma Chao thrust him from his horse with a single stroke of the spear. Ma Chao reined in his horse and turned back. Seeing that Wang Fang had been stabbed to death, Li Meng galloped after Ma Chao from behind. Ma Chao pretended not to notice. From the entrance to his formation Ma Teng shouted, “Someone is pursuing you from behind!” Before the cry had died away, Ma Chao had already seized Li Meng and held him across his horse. In truth, Ma Chao knew perfectly well that Li Meng was pursuing him but deliberately lingered. When Li Meng drew near and thrust with his spear, Ma Chao twisted aside, causing the blow to strike empty air. As the two horses came abreast, Ma Chao lightly extended his ape-like arm and captured him alive. Left without commanders, the soldiers fled at the mere sight of the enemy. Ma Teng and Han Sui seized the advantage and pursued, winning a great victory. They pressed straight to the pass and encamped beneath it, then beheaded Li Meng and displayed his head as a warning.

p.src: When Li Jue and Guo Si learned that both Li Meng and Wang Fang had been killed by Ma Chao, they finally acknowledged Jia Xu’s foresight and followed his plan closely. They concerned themselves only with guarding the pass, and however the enemy challenged them, they refused to come out and engage. Sure enough, in less than two months the Xiliang army ran short of all provisions and began discussing a retreat. Just then, a servant of Ma Yu’s household in Chang’an denounced his master, revealing that Ma Yu, Liu Fan, and Chong Shao had secretly allied themselves with Ma Teng and Han Sui outside the city and intended to serve as their agents within. Li Jue and Guo Si flew into a rage, arrested every member of the three households, young and old, free and enslaved, and executed them in the marketplace. They then brought the three severed heads directly before the gate and displayed them as a warning. With their provisions exhausted and their allies within the city exposed, Ma Teng and Han Sui had no choice but to strike camp and withdraw. Li Jue and Guo Si ordered Zhang Ji to pursue Ma Teng and Fan Chou to pursue Han Sui. The Xiliang army suffered a crushing defeat. Ma Chao fought desperately in the rear guard and drove Zhang Ji back. Fan Chou pursued Han Sui and was just about to overtake him near Chencang when Han Sui reined in and called to him, “You and I are men of the same homeland. Why are you so merciless today?” Fan Chou also reined in his horse and answered, “A command from above cannot be disobeyed!” Han Sui said, “I too came here for the sake of the state. Why must you press me so relentlessly?” After hearing this, Fan Chou turned his horse around, recalled his troops to camp, and allowed Han Sui to escape.

p.src: Since Li Jue and Guo Si defeated the forces from Xiliang, none of the lords had dared challenge them. Jia Xu repeatedly urged them to pacify the people and cultivate ties with worthy and distinguished men. From then on, the court showed faint signs of revival. Unexpectedly, the Yellow Turbans rose again in Qingzhou, gathering several hundred thousand followers under a host of different chiefs and plundering innocent people. Zhu Jun, the Grand Coachman, recommended a man capable of destroying the rebels. Li Jue and Guo Si asked who the man was. Zhu Jun said, “None but Cao Mengde can destroy the rebels east of the mountains.” Li Jue asked, “Where is Mengde now?” Zhu Jun replied, “He is presently governor of Dong Commandery and commands a great many troops. If he is ordered to suppress the rebels, they can be defeated by an appointed day.” Li Jue was delighted. That very night he drafted an imperial edict and sent a messenger bearing it to Dong Commandery, ordering Cao Cao and Bao Xin, Chancellor of Jibei, to join forces against the rebels.

p.src: Having received the imperial command, Cao Cao joined Bao Xin, and together they raised their armies and attacked the rebels at Shouyang. Bao Xin charged deep into the enemy ranks and was slain by the rebels. Cao Cao pursued the rebel army as far as Jibei, and tens of thousands surrendered. Cao Cao at once used the surrendered rebels as his vanguard; wherever his forces went, all submitted. In little more than a hundred days, he accepted the surrender of over three hundred thousand soldiers and more than a million men and women. Cao Cao selected the finest among them and named them the “Qingzhou Army”; all the rest he sent back to farming. From that time onward, Cao Cao’s power and renown grew daily. When the report of victory reached Chang’an, the court promoted Cao Cao to General Who Guards the East.

p.src: In Yanzhou, Cao Cao recruited worthy men and welcomed scholars into his service. An uncle and nephew came to join him. The uncle was a native of Yingyin in Yingchuan, surnamed Xun, named Yu, and styled Wenruo, the son of Xun Kun. He had formerly served Yuan Shao but had now left him to join Cao Cao. Cao Cao was greatly pleased after speaking with him and said, “Here is my Zhang Liang!” He thereupon appointed him Mobile Army Major. His nephew Xun You, styled Gongda, was a renowned scholar throughout the realm. He had once been appointed Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gate, but later resigned and returned home. Now he joined Cao Cao together with his uncle, and Cao Cao made him Instructor to the Marching Army. Xun Yu said, “I have heard that there is a worthy man in Yanzhou, though I do not know where he is now.” Cao Cao asked who it was, and Xun Yu replied, “He is a native of Dong’e in Dong Commandery, surnamed Cheng, named Yu, and styled Zhongde.” Cao Cao said, “I too have long heard of his reputation.” He therefore sent men to make inquiries in Cheng Yu’s home district. They learned that he was studying in the mountains, and Cao Cao respectfully invited him to come. When Cheng Yu came to see him, Cao Cao was delighted. Cheng Yu said to Xun Yu, “My learning is shallow and my knowledge meager; I am unworthy of your recommendation. A man from your own district, surnamed Guo, named Jia, and styled Fengxiao, is one of the worthy men of our age. Why not seek him out and bring him here?” Xun Yu suddenly remembered and exclaimed, “I had nearly forgotten him!” He thereupon advised Cao Cao to summon Guo Jia to Yanzhou, where they discussed the affairs of the realm together. Guo Jia recommended a direct descendant of Emperor Guangwu, a native of Chengde in Huainan, surnamed Liu, named Ye, and styled Ziyang. Cao Cao immediately invited Liu Ye to come. Liu Ye in turn recommended two men. One was a native of Changyi in Shanyang, surnamed Man, named Chong, and styled Boning. The other was a native of Wucheng, surnamed Lü, named Qian, and styled Zike. Cao Cao had long known the reputations of both men, so he invited them to serve as officers in his army. Man Chong and Lü Qian together recommended another man, a native of Pingqiu in Chenliu, surnamed Mao, named Jie, and styled Xiaoxian. Cao Cao also invited him to serve as an officer. Another commander came with several hundred soldiers to join Cao Cao. He was a native of Juping in Taishan, surnamed Yu, named Jin, and styled Wenze. Seeing that he was highly skilled with bow and horse and outstanding in martial arts, Cao Cao appointed him Major Who Commands the Army.

p.src: One day, Xiahou Dun brought a powerfully built man to see Cao Cao. When Cao Cao asked who he was, Xiahou Dun replied, “This man is a native of Chenliu, surnamed Dian, named Wei, and possessed of extraordinary strength. He formerly followed Zhang Miao, but after quarreling with men under his command and killing dozens with his own hands, he fled into the mountains. While out hunting, I saw Dian Wei chase a deer across a mountain stream, and so I took him into my ranks. I have brought him especially to recommend him to you.” Cao Cao said, “Judging by this man’s mighty build, he must possess great strength.” Xiahou Dun said, “He once killed a man to avenge a friend, then carried the severed head straight through a crowded marketplace, and not one among hundreds dared approach him. The two iron halberds he now wields weigh eighty jin; he tucks them under his arms, mounts his horse, and handles them as though they were flying.” Cao Cao at once ordered Dian Wei to demonstrate. Dian Wei tucked the halberds under his arms, spurred his horse, and galloped back and forth. Suddenly, the great banner before the command tent was caught by the wind and seemed about to topple; the assembled soldiers struggled in vain to hold it steady. Dian Wei dismounted and shouted for the soldiers to stand back. Grasping the flagpole firmly with one hand, he stood amid the wind, towering and unmoved. Cao Cao exclaimed, “Here is the E’lai of ancient times!” He thereupon appointed Dian Wei Commandant Before the Tent and bestowed on him his own brocade robe, together with a fine horse and an ornamented saddle.

Dian Wei dismounted and shouted for the soldiers to stand back. Grasping the flagpole firmly with one hand, he stood amid the wind, towering and unmoved.
Cao Cao exclaimed, “Here is the E’lai of ancient times!”
He thereupon appointed Dian Wei Commandant Before the Tent and bestowed on him his own brocade robe, together with a fine horse and an ornamented saddle.

p.src: Thus Cao Cao had sagacious counselors among his civil officers and fierce generals among his warriors, and his might overawed all the lands east of the mountains. He therefore sent Ying Shao, Governor of Taishan, to Langye Commandery to escort his father, Cao Song. Cao Song had fled the troubles in Chenliu and was living in seclusion in Langye. Upon receiving the letter that day, he set out for Yanzhou with his younger brother Cao De, more than forty members of his household, over a hundred attendants, and more than a hundred carts. His road passed through Xuzhou, whose governor, Tao Qian, styled Gongzu, was a gentle, honest, and sincere man. Tao Qian had long wished to cultivate Cao Cao’s friendship but had found no occasion to do so. Learning that Cao Cao’s father was passing through, Tao Qian went beyond his borders to welcome him, bowed twice in respect, and held a lavish banquet, entertaining him for two days. When Cao Song was ready to depart, Tao Qian personally escorted him beyond the city and specially assigned Commandant Zhang Kai and five hundred troops to guard him on his journey.

p.src: Cao Song and his household traveled as far as the region between Hua and Fei. It was the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, and when a sudden downpour came, they had no choice but to seek lodging in an ancient temple. The monks admitted them. Cao Song settled his household and ordered Zhang Kai to quarter his soldiers and horses in the two side galleries. The soldiers’ clothes and gear were all soaked by the rain, and they grumbled with one voice. Zhang Kai summoned his subordinate officers to a secluded place and conspired with them, saying, “We were originally remnants of the Yellow Turbans and only reluctantly surrendered to Tao Qian, yet we have gained nothing from it. Now Cao Song has countless baggage carts. If you wish for wealth and rank, it will be easy enough: at the third watch tonight, we shall all hack our way inside, kill Cao Song’s entire household, seize their valuables, and flee together to the mountains to become outlaws. What do you think of this plan?” They all agreed. That night, the wind and rain had not ceased. As Cao Song sat awake, he suddenly heard cries erupt on every side. Cao De went out with sword in hand to see what was happening and was immediately speared to death. Cao Song hurriedly took a concubine into the rear of the abbot’s quarters, intending to climb over the wall and escape. But the concubine was too stout to get over. In his panic, Cao Song hid with her in a privy, where both were killed by the rampaging soldiers. Ying Shao escaped with his life and went to seek refuge with Yuan Shao. Zhang Kai slaughtered Cao Song’s entire household, seized their property, set fire to the temple, and fled toward Huainan with his five hundred men. A later poet wrote:

p.src: Presently, some soldiers under Ying Shao who had escaped with their lives reported the matter to Cao Cao. When Cao Cao heard the news, he collapsed to the ground weeping. Those around him helped him up. Gritting his teeth, Cao Cao said, “Tao Qian allowed his soldiers to murder my father. This is a hatred that cannot exist beneath the same heaven! I will now raise my entire army, scour Xuzhou clean, and only then shall my hatred be appeased!” He left Xun Yu and Cheng Yu with thirty thousand troops to defend the three counties of Juancheng, Fan, and Dong’e, then led all the remaining forces in a headlong march toward Xuzhou. Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin, and Dian Wei served as the vanguard. Cao Cao ordered that whenever a city was taken, all its inhabitants were to be slaughtered, to avenge his father’s death.

p.src: At that time, Bian Rang, Governor of Jiujiang and a close friend of Tao Qian, heard that Xuzhou was in peril and personally led five thousand troops to its aid. When Cao Cao heard of this, he flew into a rage and ordered Xiahou Dun to intercept and kill him on the road. At the time, Chen Gong was serving as an assistant official in Dong Commandery and was likewise a close friend of Tao Qian. Hearing that Cao Cao had raised an army to avenge his father and intended to slaughter all the common people, he hurried through the night to see him. Cao Cao knew that he had come to plead Tao Qian's cause and at first meant to refuse him an audience; yet, unable to disregard their former friendship, he had no choice but to admit him to the command tent. Chen Gong said, “I now hear that you, my lord, have brought a great army against Xuzhou to avenge your honored father and intend to slaughter the people wherever you go. I have therefore come expressly to offer you counsel. Tao Qian is a humane and honorable gentleman, not one who forgets righteousness in the pursuit of gain. Your honored father's death was the wicked deed of Zhang Kai, not Tao Qian's crime. Moreover, what grievance have you against the people of these prefectures and counties? To kill them would bring ill fortune. I beg you to think thrice before you act.” Cao Cao angrily replied, “You abandoned me and left in former days. How dare you show your face before me again? Tao Qian has slain my family; I have sworn to tear out his gall and carve out his heart to requite my hatred! You may plead Tao Qian's cause, but what can you do if I refuse to listen?” Chen Gong took his leave, sighing, “Now I have no face to show Tao Qian either!” He then spurred his horse away to join Zhang Miao, Governor of Chenliu.

p.src: Now wherever Cao Cao's great army passed, it slaughtered the people and dug open their graves. In Xuzhou, Tao Qian heard that Cao Cao had raised an army for vengeance and was massacring the people. Raising his face to heaven, he wept bitterly and cried, “I have sinned against Heaven and brought this terrible calamity upon the people of Xuzhou!” He hastily assembled all his officers to deliberate. Cao Bao said, “Now that Cao Cao's troops have come, how can we simply fold our hands and await death? I am willing to help you defeat them, my lord.” Tao Qian had no choice but to lead his troops out to meet the enemy. From afar, Cao Cao's army looked like spreading frost and surging snow. In the center stood two white banners bearing in great characters the words “Avenge the Wrong and Wipe Away the Hatred.” The soldiers and horsemen drew up in battle formation. Cao Cao galloped out before the ranks, dressed all in white mourning garments, and raised his whip as he shouted abuse. Tao Qian also rode out beneath the gate banner, bowed in the saddle, and said, “My intention was to form friendly relations with you, my lord, and that was why I entrusted Zhang Kai with the escort. I never imagined that his brigand heart remained unchanged and that this disaster would result. In truth, it was no doing of mine. I beg you, my lord, to judge the matter clearly.” Cao Cao cursed him loudly: “You old villain! You murdered my father, and still you dare spout such nonsense! Who will take this old brigand alive?” Xiahou Dun immediately rode forth in answer. Tao Qian fled back into his ranks in alarm. Xiahou Dun pursued him, but Cao Bao leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and came forward to meet him. Just as their horses met, a furious wind suddenly arose, driving sand through the air and sending stones tumbling. Both armies fell into disorder, and each side withdrew its troops.

p.src: After returning to the city, Tao Qian consulted with the others and said, “Cao Cao's army is too powerful to resist. I shall bind myself and go to his camp, letting him cut me apart as he pleases, so that the lives of Xuzhou's people may be spared.” Before he had finished speaking, one man stepped forward and said, “Your lordship has governed Xuzhou for many years, and the people are grateful for your kindness. Though Cao Cao's troops are numerous, they have not yet succeeded in breaching our city. Your lordship and the people must hold fast within and not go forth. Though I possess little talent, I am willing to employ a modest stratagem that will leave Cao Cao without a place to bury his corpse!” Everyone was astonished and immediately asked what plan he proposed. And so it is said:
